query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, controlled heat treatment promotes diffusion‐driven partitioning of key elements (especially Al, and, if present, Ti) that nucleates and stabilizes coherent γ′‐like precipitates. This phase separation mediates the interplay between solid‐solution strengthening and precipitate strengthening, thereby governing phase stability and enabling the alloy to retain high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, solution annealed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy (optionally with minor Ti addition) with a uniform solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Aging treatment at a controlled temperature (e.g., 750°C) for varying durations to induce precipitate nucleation and growth.
generation.conditions: Isothermal aging at 750°C with systematic variation of the treatment time; testing conducted under high-temperature, cryogenic, and radiation exposure conditions to assess multi-functional performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The volume fraction, size distribution, and composition (notably enrichment in Al/Ti) of the γ′-like precipitates within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Diffusion-controlled elemental partitioning during aging leads to nucleation and coherent growth of precipitates. These precipitates, via interfacial strengthening and dislocation pinning, stabilize the phase structure against coarsening and transform the mechanical response across a range of temperatures while maintaining environmental and radiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline solution annealed state, the aged alloy will display a microstructure with a significant, well-dispersed precipitate phase that correlates with increased yield strength at high temperatures, preserved or enhanced toughness at cryogenic temperatures, and improved resistance to environmental degradation.
generation.baseline: The as-solution annealed alloy with a homogeneous single-phase solid solution lacking the precipitate microstructure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys (potentially with minor Ti for precipitate stabilization) under controlled aging conditions; deviations in alloying elements or non-isothermal processing may lead to different phase behaviors and cannot be inferred by this mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed kinetics of elemental partitioning and precipitation, as well as the exact contribution of other minor elements (if present) on phase stability and multi-functional properties, remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys (with optional minor Ti addition): one set maintained in the solution annealed condition (baseline) and another subjected to aging at 750°C for a time calculated to induce significant precipitate formation. Characterize both sets using electron microscopy techniques (SEM, TEM, atom probe tomography) to quantify precipitate volume fraction, size, and elemental segregation. Perform mechanical tests (yield strength, toughness tests over high-temperature and cryogenic conditions) and expose samples to radiation and corrosive environments.
measurements: Quantitative microstructural analysis (e.g., precipitate volume fraction, size distribution, and chemical mapping)
Yield strength and tensile tests at high and cryogenic temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in precipitate formation in accordance with the expected Al/Ti partitioning and, more importantly, fails to exhibit the corresponding enhancements in yield strength, toughness, and resistance relative to the baseline solution annealed alloy, then the hypothesis that precipitation-mediated phase stabilization governs the desired multi-functional property retention in these HEAs will be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThe efficient energy use in multiple sectors of modern industry is partly based on the efficient use of high-strength, high-performance alloys that retain remarkable mechanical properties at elevated and high temperatures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent the most recent class of these materials with a high potential for high-temperature high-strength applications. Aside from their chemical composition and microstructure-property relationship, limited information on the effect of heat treatment as a decisive factor for alloy design is available in the literature. This work intends to contribute to this research topic by investigating the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance of an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 HEA. The solution annealed state is compared to aged states obtained at different heat treatment times at 750 °C. The temporal evolution of the matrix and the γ’-precipitates are analyzed in terms of chemical composition, crystallography, size, shape, and volume fraction by means of scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography.
